best_for: Raspberry Pi tinkerers and anyone making a Linux install stick who wants to write an image to an SD card or USB drive without the risk of wiping the wrong disk.

points.title: Three clicks, no command line
points.text: Pick an image, pick a drive, press Flash. It writes OS images to SD cards and USB drives and makes boot media from ISO files. You avoid typing a `dd` command where one wrong letter erases a disk.

points.title: Checks its own work
points.text: After writing, Etcher reads the card back to confirm the copy is good, so a bad card or failed write shows up now and not at first boot.

points.title: Hides your system drive
points.text: System drives are hidden by default and you get a warning before writing to anything that looks risky. That makes it hard to overwrite your own computer's disk by mistake.

points.title: Free and open source
points.text: balenaEtcher costs nothing and is released under the Apache 2.0 license. There is no account to create.

points.title: Intel 64-bit only on Windows and Linux
points.text: Windows needs version 10 or later on x64, with no Arm build. Windows 7, 8 and 32-bit systems top out at Etcher 7.9.0. The Windows installer sets it up for the current user, and this listing keeps 40 versions.

points.title: Mac and Linux
points.text: The Mac downloads come as separate Intel and Apple silicon builds, and only the current release is listed here. Linux users can get .deb and .rpm packages from the project's GitHub releases; this site does not list them.
